title: Two Notes at Once
description: Hold two keys together and hear how the distance between them changes the sound. It's your first step toward chords.

steps.title: Why two notes?
steps.description: When two notes sound together, the distance between them is called an interval. Some intervals sound tight and buzzy, others open and calm. Chords are just intervals stacked up, so getting comfortable with pairs makes chords much easier later.

steps.title: C and D
steps.description: Hold C4 and D4 together. Neighboring white keys like these make a major second. It sounds a little rubbed together, slightly tense.
steps.hint: Use your thumb and index finger and press both at the same moment.

steps.title: C and E
steps.description: Now hold C4 and E4. This is a major third. Hear how much sweeter and brighter it is than the second.
steps.hint: Skip one white key: C, (D), E.

steps.title: C and G
steps.description: Hold C4 and G4. This is a perfect fifth, a wide and open sound. Rock guitarists build their power chords on it.
steps.hint: Thumb on C, pinky on G. That's five white keys, counting both ends.

steps.title: E and A
steps.description: Try E4 and A4. This is a perfect fourth. It's open like the fifth, but it feels a little less settled.
steps.hint: Count four white keys starting from E: E, F, G, A.

steps.title: D and B
steps.description: Hold D4 and B4, a major sixth. It's a wider stretch, with a warm, sweet sound you'll hear in lots of melodies.
steps.hint: Count six white keys from D up to B. Thumb on D, pinky on B.

steps.title: Name that interval
steps.description: You played C and G together a moment ago. What's that interval called?
